Instituted in the 15th–16th century; a UNESCO-recognised living tradition

venues.name: Sri Harmandir Sahib (The Golden Temple)
venues.note: The gilded sanctum floats at the centre of the Amrit Sarovar, its reflection breaking gently on the water while unbroken kirtan drifts across the marble. For a Sikh-heritage family it is the still point of the whole journey; for anyone it is one of the most moving spaces in India.

venues.name: The Parikrama
venues.note: The white marble walkway that rings the sarovar, walked barefoot and clockwise, past pilgrims, gilt-edged shrines and the slow ripple of the tank. A private guide who knows where to pause turns a circuit into a reading of five centuries of Sikh history.

venues.name: The Akal Takht
venues.note: The seat of temporal Sikh authority, facing the Harmandir Sahib across the causeway, where the community's edicts have been issued since 1606. Standing before it explains the Sikh idea that the spiritual and the political are one.

venues.name: The Amrit Sarovar (Holy Tank)
venues.note: The pool of nectar that gives Amritsar its name, its steps worn smooth by generations who bathe here at dawn. Sitting at the water's edge in the quiet before sunrise is the single most peaceful hour the city offers.

venues.name: The Palki Sahib Ceremony (Night)
venues.note: Each night the Guru Granth Sahib is carried on a silver-and-gold palanquin from the sanctum to the Akal Takht amid rosewater and shouldered devotion, the Sukhasan ritual ending around 9:30-10 PM. Attending it, then again the Prakash before dawn, bookends a stay in something unforgettable.

venues.name: Dawn Darshan & The Prakash Ceremony
venues.note: In the dark small hours the Guru Granth Sahib is installed in the sanctum and the first hymns rise as the sky lightens over the gold. Arriving at 3-4 AM with a guide who can move you through the crowd is a rare, unhurried privilege.

venues.name: The Langar (Guru Ka Langar)
venues.note: The world's largest free community kitchen feeds up to a hundred thousand people a day, everyone seated on the floor as equals. Rolling rotis alongside the sevadars for an hour is a humbling, hands-on experience that stays with multi-generational travellers.

venues.name: Central Sikh Museum
venues.note: Above the main entrance to the complex, galleries of Guru portraits, martyr paintings, arms and rare manuscripts trace the faith's history and its long line of sacrifice. A quiet, weighty counterpoint to the devotion outside, and free to enter.

venues.name: Gurdwara Baba Atal Rai
venues.note: A nine-storey octagonal tower beside the Golden Temple, its walls once painted with frescoes of Guru Nanak's life, built in memory of Guru Hargobind's young son. Fewer visitors climb it, and the rooftop gives a rare high view over the sanctum and the old city.

venues.name: Jallianwala Bagh
venues.note: The walled garden where, in 1919, General Dyer's troops fired on a peaceful gathering; the bullet-marked wall and the martyrs' well remain, now within a renovated memorial complex with galleries and a light-and-sound show. A short walk from the Golden Temple and essential to understanding modern India.

venues.name: Partition Museum
venues.note: Housed in the restored colonial Town Hall, this is the world's first museum dedicated to the 1947 Partition, told through survivor testimony, personal objects and letters. For Punjabi families whose grandparents crossed the new border, it is often the most personal stop in the city.

venues.name: Attari-Wagah Border Beating Retreat
venues.note: The daily lowering-of-the-flags ceremony where Indian and Pakistani guards high-kick and posture as the crowd roars, held at the last checkpost before Lahore around 6 PM. Reserve VIP seating near the gate; the patriotism is unabashed and children love it.

venues.name: Gobindgarh Fort
venues.note: Maharaja Ranjit Singh's military fort, once the treasury of the Koh-i-Noor, reopened as a living-history complex with the Sher-e-Punjab 7D show, the Toshakhana turban museum, artisans and folk performers. A full evening's outing that works well across three generations.

venues.name: Kandha Boldiyan Ne (Whispering Walls) Show
venues.note: The nightly sound-and-light spectacle projected onto the fort's ramparts, telling the story of the fort and Ranjit Singh's Sikh empire after dark. Book the 8 PM show and pair it with an early dinner inside the fort's dhaba court.

venues.name: Durgiana Temple
venues.note: A Hindu temple to Durga and Lakshmi built in the 1920s in the very image of the Golden Temple, gilded and set in its own tank. It gives a fuller sense of Amritsar as a shared sacred city, and is far quieter than its famous cousin.

venues.name: Ram Tirath Temple
venues.note: The reputed hermitage of sage Valmiki, where legend places the birth of Luv and Kush and the writing of the Ramayana, marked by an ancient tank and a colossal Valmiki statue. A peaceful, mythic day-side detour that most tourists miss entirely.

venues.name: Maharaja Ranjit Singh Museum & Summer Palace
venues.note: The Lion of Punjab's own summer palace, set in the Ram Bagh gardens, now displaying his arms, armour, coins, miniatures and a panorama of the Sikh court. The best single place to meet the man whose empire made Amritsar, and to walk his gardens after.

venues.name: Ram Bagh Garden (Company Bagh)
venues.note: The formal garden Ranjit Singh laid out on the model of Lahore's Shalimar, with pavilions, a summer palace and old shade trees in the heart of the city. A cool, green interval between the intensity of the shrines.

venues.name: Amritsar Heritage Walk (Old City)
venues.note: A guided route through the 400-year-old walled city, from the Town Hall through the katras and akharas to the Golden Temple, past frescoed havelis, the old mint and hidden shrines. A private early-morning walk, before the crowds, is the finest way to read the real Amritsar.

venues.name: Chitta Akhara
venues.note: A monastic complex from 1781 on the heritage walk, prized for its delicate Rajasthani-influenced wall paintings tucked deep in the lanes. The kind of place only a good local guide will open for you.

venues.name: Kesar Da Dhaba
venues.note: Serving since 1916 in a narrow old-city lane, famous for dal makhani slow-cooked overnight in a brass pot over wood flame, lachha parathas and firni. The unshowy, definitive Amritsari meal; a guide can arrange a quiet table away from the queue.
credentials: Established 1916, a living Amritsar institution
The Better India / Slurrp, favoured by Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Lala Lajpat Rai
Condé Nast Traveller India, Amritsar must-visit

venues.name: Bharawan Da Dhaba
venues.note: A pre-Partition institution (since 1912) near the Town Hall, turning out tandoor-fresh kulchas, dahi bhalla and chole for the better part of a century. Vegetarian, generous and a fixture of any Amritsari food pilgrimage.
credentials: Established 1912, Amritsar's oldest dhaba
YourStory / Slurrp, a century-old Amritsar institution
A ten-minute walk from the Golden Temple

venues.name: Amritsari Kulcha (The Dish)
venues.note: The city's signature: a potato-and-spice-stuffed flatbread crisped in a tandoor, cracked open with white butter and dark chole. Worth eating at more than one address, kulcha crawl style, to argue over who does it best.

venues.name: Kulcha Land
venues.note: A cleaner, sit-down alternative to the old-city dhabas on the newer Lawrence Road, doing crisp stuffed kulchas washed down with lassi. Useful when travelling with elders who want the flavour without the crush.

venues.name: Sadda Pind
venues.note: A twelve-acre recreation of a 19th-century Punjabi village, with mud homes, artisans, Gatka, Bhangra, bioscope and a full Punjabi buffet. A curated, comfortable way to give children and grandparents the rural Punjab their family came from; overnight stays exist for the fully immersed.

venues.name: Khalsa College
venues.note: A 300-acre campus of magnificent Indo-Saracenic architecture designed by Bhai Ram Singh in 1892, its main building a favourite of film crews. A short stop for the scale and the beauty of the facade, and for the story of Sikh self-assertion under the Raj.

venues.name: Gurdwara Baba Deep Singh Shaheedan Sahib
venues.note: The shrine marking where the 75-year-old warrior-scholar Baba Deep Singh fell in 1757 defending the desecrated Golden Temple, one of Sikhism's most revered martyrdom sites. A powerful, less-visited stop for those tracing the faith's history of sacrifice.

venues.name: Gurdwara Chheharta Sahib
venues.note: Built where Guru Arjan Dev sank a great well fed by six Persian wheels, giving the town its name; the sixth Guru was born nearby. A calm, historic gurdwara on the way to the Wagah border, easy to fold into that afternoon.

venues.name: Hall Bazaar
venues.note: The oldest, busiest market in the city, entered through a Mughal-style gateway, stacked with phulkari, Punjabi juttis, dry fruit and handicrafts. A guide can steer you to the trusted old houses for embroidery and footwear worth carrying home.

venues.name: Katra Jaimal Singh Market
venues.note: The textile heart of Amritsar, its lanes lined with shops for suits, sarees and wedding fabric at prices that surprise. Punjabi families still come here to buy trousseaux; a knowledgeable escort makes the bargaining painless.

venues.name: Papad-Warian Lanes (Majith Mandi)
venues.note: The alleys where sun-dried Amritsari papad and spiced lentil warian are made and sold, the smell of asafoetida hanging in the air. A quick, sensory old-city errand that yields the most authentic edible souvenir of Punjab.

venues.name: Punjabi Jutti Shopping
venues.note: Amritsar's hand-embroidered leather juttis are among the finest in India, made by families who have stitched them for generations. Commissioning a bespoke pair, or fitting the whole family, is a small, memorable indulgence.

venues.name: Pul Kanjari
venues.note: A little pleasure-stop Maharaja Ranjit Singh built for his dancer Moran, complete with baoli, temple, mosque and gurdwara side by side as a mark of his secular rule. A poignant, near-empty ruin best paired with the Wagah ceremony the same afternoon.

venues.name: Gurdwara Tarn Taran Sahib
venues.note: Founded by Guru Arjan Dev, this gurdwara holds the largest sarovar of any Sikh shrine, thronged on the monthly Amavas. A serene, grand day-trip that rewards early arrival, well short of the tourist trail.

venues.name: Sri Khadoor Sahib
venues.note: The home town of the second Guru, Angad Dev, where he formalised the Gurmukhi script and where Mata Khivi ran an early langar. Part of the classic three-gurdwara heritage circuit south of the city, rich in the faith's formative story.

venues.name: Pingalwara
venues.note: Bhagat Puran Singh's home for the destitute, sick and abandoned, a byword in Punjab for selfless service. A visit, or a quiet contribution, gives a stay a dimension of seva beyond the shrines and the food.

venues.name: Saragarhi Memorial Gurdwara
venues.note: A memorial to the 21 Sikh soldiers who fought to the last man at Saragarhi in 1897, one of history's most celebrated last stands. Small but stirring, and close enough to the Golden Temple to see in the same morning.

venues.name: Amritsar Food Trail (Guided)
venues.note: A curated crawl through the old-city lanes taking in kulcha, lassi, fish tikka, jalebi and kada prasad in a single morning, led by someone who knows every counter. The most delicious way to understand why food is half the reason to come to Amritsar.

venues.name: Makhan Fish & Chicken Corner
venues.note: For the non-vegetarians, the city's most famous Amritsari fish tikka, batter-fried in the winter season and eaten hot off the tawa. A savoury counterpoint for families who want more than the vegetarian dhaba canon.
credentials: A recognised Amritsar culinary icon (since the 1960s–90s lineage)
Renowned for Amritsari fish (singhara / sohal) and tandoori chicken

venues.name: Jalianwala Bagh Light & Sound Show
venues.note: The evening projection within the renovated memorial that narrates the 1919 massacre against the bullet-scarred walls. An emotive way to close a day begun at the Golden Temple, and a chance to sit with the history rather than pass through it.

venues.name: Golden Temple Roof & Sunset Views
venues.note: As the light softens, the gold catches fire and the reflection in the sarovar deepens; the langar hall roof and the parikrama's far side give the calmest vantage. Timing a slow evening circuit for golden hour is the photograph everyone remembers.

venues.name: Qila Ahluwalia & The Old City Gates
venues.note: Fragments of the fort of the Ahluwalia misl and the surviving gateways of the walled city, woven into the heritage walk, mark the boundary of eighteenth-century Amritsar. Small architectural clues that make the whole old city legible once a guide points them out.

venues.name: The bar at Taj Swarna
venues.note: The most composed evening drink in a modest city, Taj service, well-kept spirits and quiet.
credentials: Inside Taj Swarna, Taj Hotels' Amritsar flagship

venues.name: Rooftop cafés overlooking the Golden Temple
venues.note: Not a bar but the city's real night view, chai or a cold coffee above the illuminated temple, mirrored in its pool.
credentials: Rooftop cafés on the Golden Temple heritage plaza
The definitive Amritsar evening view, the lit temple after dark
